note: Reel 49: The Con. Script draft 3 (approved by the user through HQ, 23 Nov: 'Yes, the thief'). The narrator is the series voice (af_heart, 1.0; takes 2-3 at 0.96 and 1.04). The thief never speaks. The uncle (u*) and the new chaiwala at the next stall (c01) are auditioned in a cast run (six male voices; reel 25 found am_onyx, am_michael and am_adam clean; hm_omega read a TV line clean in reel 40) and read straight from it. Every line is one breath; a count that needs a real pause is its own line, placed on its note's slap (pauses are set by hand, never edited inside a line). Variants (b, c): hand-planned phonemes for the Indian words (chaiwala, rupee, Arre) and the cut-off count; Kokoro's Hindi voices read phoneme markup aloud, so their variants are plain spellings. Facts: docs/research.md. Round 2 (23 Nov): the cast run picked am_michael for the uncle (creak near 0, 'Arre' planned as /əɹˈA/ heard as 'Array', which is the sound) and am_onyx for the next stall's chaiwala; 'Four-sev' came out /sˈAv/ ('save'), so u05c plans it by hand, in am_michael only.
ref_text: The night was cold and very quiet. Most of the street was asleep, and the lamps hummed over the empty road. Somewhere far away, a train rolled past, and then the silence came back.

lines.text: He's about to con the chaiwala.
He's about to con the chaiwala.
Five hundred? For a ten-rupee chai?
Five hundred? For a ten-rupee chai?
Oh, you have change? Then take your five hundred back.
His five hundred came down, and the uncle counted out four-fifty.
Then a ten for the chai, and his five hundred went back.
lines.text_kokoro: Then a ten for the [chai](/ʧˈI/), and his five hundred went back.

lines.text: But one raised eyebrow, and the uncle counted on: four-seventy, four-ninety.
The uncle counted it all out for him.
Your brain can only hold about four things at once, so he kept handing the uncle one more.
That's why police tell shopkeepers: one deal at a time.
Five hundred? For a ten-rupee chai?
